Coxeter Tangent Circles

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Three circles touch each other, and a fourth circle fits in the gap; another set of four circles touches at the very same six spots.
How to play: Drag the dots A, B and C, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Pick the inner or outer circle and press the buttons to show or hide the extra circles and spots.
Look for the math

Drag any centre and every circle changes size. Yet the six places where the circles touch keep their pattern, and another four circles can always be drawn through them. Why?

Three circles that touch

Let the three circles have radii ra, rb, rc and centres A, B, C. Because they touch, the sides of the triangle of centres are

a = BC = rb + rc,  b = CA = rc + ra,  c = AB = ra + rb

The page then writes a = x + y, b = y + z, c = z + x for the lengths from the corners to the touching points. Adding the first and third equations and subtracting the second gives 2x = a + c − b, and the other two unknowns follow in the same way. The coefficient matrix has determinant 2, so the answer is unique: with these side labels x = rb, y = rc, z = ra — exactly the three radii.

Where the tangents meet

The common tangent at each touching point is perpendicular to the line joining the two centres. The three tangents meet at one point with equal tangent lengths to all three circles: the radical centre. Since the lines of centres form the triangle above, that point is also its incenter.

d(O, A)² − ra² = d(O, B)² − rb² = d(O, C)² − rc² = r²

Here r is the radius of the incircle of the triangle of centres. The equation says the incircle passes through the three touching points and meets each original circle at right angles. The logic test checked that the radical centre really is the incenter, that the three powers are equal, and that the orthogonality equation holds for over a thousand configurations.

Two quadruplets of four

Philip Beecroft's theorem says that if four circles all touch each other, a second set of four can be drawn whose six touching points are the same. Here the fourth circle is either the small one in the gap or the enclosing one; the other four are the incircle plus one circle through each pair of touching points. The applet finds the fourth circle by solving two linear equations for its centre and one quadratic for its radius, the same equations behind Descartes' theorem. The test compares that calculation instruction by instruction with the Java bytecode, then checks all six pairs of the second family for a shared point and tangency, in both families.

The cut-the-knot page still embeds the Java program, so its rules and five controls are kept. Two harmless applet details stay: GetCircle averages its three distances from the circumcentre (they are equal when the points are exact), and CommonPoint ignores its third argument. The enclosing circle can touch an inner circle from the outside in some positions; the test accepts either kind of contact. Only the presentation changed: modern SVG, focusable dots and site colours instead of AWT panels.

Tick Ortho family and Tangencies, then switch between Inner circle and Outer circle. Each of the four new circles passes through three of the six dots, and neighbouring new circles touch at one dot.
